summary:
Lost in Space is an interactive 3D digital museum that brings forgotten spacecraft and abandoned space hardware back to life. It explores the legacy of human space exploration through four exhibition zones: the Moon, Mars, Earth orbit and deep space.

The platform features a curated collection of 26 space artifacts, supported by more than 66 source-linked facts, NASA archival imagery and interactive 3D spacecraft models. Users can explore a 3D solar-system map, discover each artifact's mission history, investigate why it was left behind, compare spacecraft and interact with a source-grounded Mission AI assistant.

Designed to make complex space-history archives more accessible to students, particularly learners in Grades 6–12, Lost in Space transforms fragmented technical records into engaging, educational experiences.

Its central idea is simple: spacecraft may fall silent or become inactive, but their scientific contributions and stories should not be forgotten.
details:
Lost in Space — An Interactive 3D Museum of Abandoned Spacecraft

Project Overview

Lost in Space is an interactive educational platform that transforms historical records of abandoned, inactive and discarded space hardware into an immersive digital museum.

The project addresses an educational problem: information about spacecraft, their missions, scientific contributions and eventual resting places is scattered across technical catalogs, NASA archives, mission reports and historical databases. These sources are valuable but can be difficult for students and the general public to navigate.

Lost in Space brings this information together through an interactive 3D solar-system experience.

How It Works

The application organizes its curated collection into four exhibition zones:

  • The Moon — lunar landers, spacecraft and equipment left behind.
  • Mars — rovers, landers and other planetary exploration hardware.
  • Earth Orbit — satellites, space stations and inactive orbital objects.
  • Deep Space — probes and spacecraft travelling beyond Earth.

Users explore an interactive 3D solar-system map, select individual spacecraft and open detailed mission exhibits.

The collection contains 26 curated artifacts, more than 66 source-linked facts and a collection of archival imagery and 3D spacecraft models.

Each exhibit explores a spacecraft's identity, mission purpose, launch, operational history, scientific discoveries, final transmission or abandonment, and known resting location.

Interactive Educational Features

1. Interactive 3D Solar System

A 3D visualization built with Three.js and React Three Fiber allows users to navigate the solar-system exhibition, select destinations and explore the locations of historical space artifacts.

2. Mission AI

Each spacecraft has a scoped educational assistant that answers questions using that artifact's stored, verified facts and mission records.

The assistant supports primary-school and high-school reading levels, provides source-linked answers and can generate quizzes. It is deliberately restricted to the selected spacecraft's available information rather than freely inventing mission facts.

3. Narrated Mission Experiences

Narrated photo experiences and voice-guided educational content help users explore historical NASA imagery and mission timelines.

4. Zone Science Labs

Interactive educational workspaces provide hands-on exploration of lunar and Martian environments and mission-related science.

5. Spacecraft Comparison

Users can compare selected artifacts, inspect their specifications, examine differences and explore relationships between hardware and missions.

6. Live Orbital Tracking

Selected Earth-orbit objects can be connected to orbital element data and propagated positions using CelesTrak OMM data and SGP4 calculations.

Data and Scientific Reliability

The project combines several information sources, including NASA's Space Science Data Coordinated Archive, NASA mission pages, NASA Image and Video Library, NASA 3D Resources, JPL Horizons and the General Catalog of Artificial Space Objects.

Every curated fact has source provenance. Images and 3D assets retain their individual credits and licensing information.

The project follows an important architectural principle: the database owns the facts, while any generated narration is separate from the underlying scientific record. This helps prevent generated explanations from silently becoming authoritative mission data.

Technology

The application uses:

  • Next.js 15, React and TypeScript for the web application.
  • Three.js and React Three Fiber for interactive 3D visualization.
  • MapLibre GL JS for geographical mapping.
  • PostgreSQL 16 for structured space-artifact data.
  • Python and psycopg for data ingestion and ETL.
  • satellite.js for orbital calculations.
  • CelesTrak OMM data for selected Earth-orbit tracking.
  • Web Speech API for browser-based voice experiences.
  • Render for deployment and hosting.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Lost in Space aims to make space exploration history more accessible, especially to Grade 6–12 learners.

It helps students understand not only what spacecraft achieved, but also why they were launched, how they operated, what they discovered and why some were ultimately left behind.

By combining 3D visualization, interactive learning, sourced scientific information and educational AI capabilities, the project transforms static technical archives into a more engaging learning environment.

What Makes It Different

Lost in Space treats abandoned spacecraft as physical artifacts with histories, identities and relationships rather than isolated objects in a catalog.

Its creative approach combines a digital museum, solar-system exploration, source-grounded educational assistance and interactive mission storytelling.

The result is an experience where every forgotten spacecraft becomes an opportunity to learn about humanity's journey into space.
